scenes.heading: CAP Theorem
scenes.narration: The CAP theorem states that in the presence of a network partition, a distributed data store can guarantee only two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance at once.

scenes.heading: The three properties
bullets: Consistency: every read sees the latest write
Availability: every request gets a non-error response
Partition tolerance: the system survives dropped messages
Under a partition you must sacrifice C or A
scenes.narration: Consistency means every read returns the most recent write or an error, so all nodes agree. Availability means every request receives a non-error response, even if it is not the newest data. Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating despite messages being lost between nodes. Because partitions are unavoidable in real networks, the real choice under a partition is between consistency and availability.

scenes.heading: Why P is not optional
bullets: Networks drop and delay messages in reality
The genuine choice is only C versus A
scenes.narration: A common misreading of CAP is that you freely pick any two of the three properties. In practice, partition tolerance is not optional, because real networks inevitably drop, delay, and reorder messages, and hardware fails unpredictably. A distributed system that could not tolerate partitions would simply be unavailable the moment the network hiccupped. So partition tolerance is a given, and the genuine engineering decision is only how you behave during a partition, trading consistency against availability.

scenes.heading: What happens during a partition
steps: Network splits the cluster in two
CP side blocks or errors to stay consistent
AP side answers with local, possibly stale data
scenes.narration: Picture a network partition that splits the cluster into two isolated groups that can no longer talk. Both sides keep receiving client requests. A CP system on either side will block or return errors rather than risk diverging, sacrificing availability to protect consistency. An AP system instead answers from its local replica with possibly stale data, staying available but risking conflicting views. When the partition finally heals, the replicas must reconcile any divergence before returning to normal.

scenes.heading: Choosing under a partition

left.label: CP system
points: Rejects or blocks writes to stay consistent

scenes.narration: A CP system refuses or blocks requests it cannot answer consistently, so callers may see errors during a partition, but the data they do get is always correct; ZooKeeper and HBase behave this way. An AP system always answers, even if the value is stale, which keeps the service up but risks conflicting reads; Cassandra and DynamoDB take this path. Choose CP when correctness is non-negotiable, like ledgers, and AP when availability matters more, like a shopping cart.

scenes.heading: PACELC extends CAP
bullets: If Partitioned, choose Availability or Consistency
Explains tradeoffs even with no partition
Dynamo is PA/EL, a strict RDBMS is PC/EC
scenes.narration: PACELC extends CAP to describe behavior even when the network is healthy. It says that if there is a Partition you trade Availability against Consistency, but Else, in normal operation, you still trade Latency against Consistency. This matters because strong consistency requires coordination that adds latency every day, not just during rare partitions. A system like Dynamo is PA and EL, favoring availability and low latency, while a strict relational database is PC and EC, favoring consistency in both regimes.

scenes.text: CAP forces a conscious C-versus-A tradeoff only during partitions; design each service around which it can least afford to lose.
scenes.narration: CAP does not mean you pick two properties forever; it means that during a network partition you must consciously trade consistency against availability, so design each service around whichever it can least afford to lose.
